sections.sectionText: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION & HERITAGE INTERPRETATION: Environmental Educators and Interpreters connect visitors to important natural, cultural, and historical resources at parks, nature centers, historical sites, aquariums, zoos, museums, or anywhere people come to learn and have meaningful experiences at these sites. This course introduces students to the basic principles of interpretation & environmental education; techniques to make programs purposeful, enjoyable, relevant, organized, and thematic; characteristics of audiences; non-personal interpretation; and the basics of project management and grant writing. The course will combine theoretical foundations with practical skills. Field trips will be during class time; transportation will be provided to off-campus sites. A final presentation to a public audience is scheduled for Saturday May 1. This section will have a field trip fee of $75. Students from majors other than NRES may complete the form at http://go.illinois.edu/NREScourserequests to be added to the wait list.

sections.sectionText: FIELD PRACTICES FOR FOREST MANAGEMENT: This field-based course will introduce students to practices used in forest management and restoration, including prescribed fire, invasive species control, and safe use of chainsaws. Learning and application of techniques will occur via instruction, demonstration, and hands-on practice at the Dixon Springs Agricultural Center (DSAC) during spring break from March 15-19, 2027. There are three mandatory on-campus meetings prior to the field trip: February 17, February 24, and March 3. All campus meetings will be in N-120 Turner Hall at 4 p.m. This section has a field trip fee of $125 that will be charged to the student account. If all seats are full, complete the form at http://go.illinois.edu/NREScourserequests to be added to the wait list.

sections.sectionText: Fish & Wildlife Field Techniques will meet in person for several sessions during the second half of the semester and also during the week of May 17-21 (students are responsible for their own housing). Field work will occur at Allerton Park in Monticello, IL (transportation provided) and we will spend one night on-site in 4H housing. This course will introduce students to techniques used in monitoring and research within the disciplines of fishery resources and wildlife ecology/management. We will focus on survey methods including sampling, capturing, handling and marking wildlife (mammals, birds, fish, aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, and reptiles). The field exercises will allow students to gain exposure and hands-on experience with commonly used techniques. The students will also use data from the monitoring to provide a group presentation on developing a monitoring protocol for a specific taxa. This section will have a field trip fee of $130. If all seats are full, complete the form at http://go.illinois.edu/NRESwaitinglist to be added to the waiting list.

Introduces students to the importance of sustainability in the Public Policymaking process with emphasis on the policies and operations of key Illinois State Agencies including but not limited to the Depts. of Natural Resources and Environmental Protections. Studies and evaluates various conceptual models and practices in sustainability public policy formulation at the state level. This course will meet in N-120 Turner Hall for the first class meeting. There will be 3 or 4 required in-person field trips that utilize the full class time. All other class meetings will occur online and will typically last 90 minutes. This section has a field trip fee of $55

This course explores natural resource management topics in the US protected area system with a particular focus on Great Smoky Mountains National Park (GSMNP). Students will meet in-person during the first half of the semester and the course will culminate in a week-long field experience held in conjunction with five other universities that will be staying at the Great Smoky Mountains Tremont Institute in Tennessee. This travel component will take place March 22-26, 2027, and requires missing other classes. The course fee for this section is $1,225 and includes transportation to and from Tennessee, as well as lodging during the week-long field trip. If all seats are full, complete the form at http://go.illinois.edu/NREScourserequests to be added to the wait list

WILDLIFE CONSERVATION & HABITAT MANAGEMENT IN SOUTH AFRICA: This course provides you with a unique understanding of the most up-to-date, in-field conservation techniques and practices, while exploring and contributing to important wildlife conservation work on the famous Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park, known to be the birthplace of modern wildlife conservation in Africa. Course meetings will take place during the second eight weeks of the spring semester. Travel dates will be in May after the conclusion of the Spring 2027 semester. Students registered in this section pay a STUDY ABROAD FEE assessed through the ACES Education Abroad Office. For additional information and the application, see: https://app.studyabroad.illinois.edu/index.cfm?FuseAction=Programs.ViewProgramAngular&id=11960

sections.sectionText: Advanced Fisheries Ecology is a graduate-level discussion course covering complex issues confronting fish conservation and fisheries management. The goals of the course are to (1) become informed on complex issues confronting fish conservation and fisheries management, (2) understand the science underpinning these issues and the various approaches used to address them, and (3) become confident in analyzing, assessing, and discussing different perspectives on contentious issues in applied ecology. PREREQUISITE: NRES 409 or an equivalent course in fisheries science from another institution. This class will meet in a classroom TBD in the Forbes Natural History Building in the University Research Park complex. Course days and times are also TBD.

sections.sectionText: This course investigates the interaction between agricultural practices and wildlife (mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians), with emphasis on how changes in Midwestern agricultural practices have affected wildlife and what the future might hold. We will also discuss sustainable management in these environments and the current trends in this field. With the advent of biofuels and new and revised USDA programs geared toward creating wildlife habitat on former agricultural fields, the overall effect of agriculture on wildlife populations may rapidly change over the next decade. These changes may be beneficial for some species, while detrimental to others. Online scheduled class sessions require each student to have high speed internet access and either a headset with microphone or an external microphone and speakers so they may participate in the class discussions. Wireless internet is not recommended.
